02 · Pandas for data handling¶

CSE273 Unit II. Series and DataFrames, reading and writing CSV, inspecting a dataset, selecting with loc / iloc, boolean filtering, and visualising with Matplotlib: line, bar, histogram, scatter and pie charts, customising plots and subplots.

In [1]:
try:
    import groundwork
except ImportError:  # running on Kaggle
    %pip install -q git+https://github.com/LuShadowX/Groundwork
    import groundwork

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from groundwork import data, plotting
plotting.setup()
COLORS = [plotting.CLASS_COLORS[c] for c in data.CLASSES]

1. Series and DataFrame¶

1.1 Series¶

A Series is a one-dimensional array with an index: every value has a label.

In [2]:
moisture = pd.Series([32.6, 56.6, 12.2, 50.3], index=["field_a", "field_b", "field_c", "field_d"], name="Soil_Moisture")
print(moisture)
print("\nfield_c:", moisture["field_c"], "| mean:", moisture.mean(), "| dtype:", moisture.dtype)
print(moisture[moisture < 40])
print((moisture / 100).round(3).to_dict())

field_b    56.6
field_c    12.2
field_d    50.3

1.2 DataFrame¶

A DataFrame is a table: columns are Series that share one index, and each column can have its own type.

In [3]:
fields = pd.DataFrame({
    "Crop_Type": ["Wheat", "Rice", "Maize", "Cotton"],
    "Soil_Moisture": moisture.to_numpy(),
    "Temperature_C": [15.0, 22.9, 34.1, 29.4],
    "Mulching_Used": [False, True, False, True],
}, index=moisture.index)
fields["Dry_and_hot"] = (fields["Soil_Moisture"] < 30) & (fields["Temperature_C"] > 30)
print(fields)
print("\n", fields.dtypes, sep="")

        Crop_Type  Soil_Moisture  Temperature_C  Mulching_Used  Dry_and_hot
field_a     Wheat           32.6           15.0          False        False
field_b      Rice           56.6           22.9           True        False
field_c     Maize           12.2           34.1          False         True
field_d    Cotton           50.3           29.4           True        False

2. Reading and writing CSV files¶

2.1 Reading CSV¶

data.load() is a thin wrapper around pd.read_csv. Here is the call itself, timed, with a few useful options:

In [4]:
import time
t = time.perf_counter()
train = pd.read_csv(data.data_dir() / "train.csv")
print(f"read {len(train):,} rows × {train.shape[1]} columns in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f} s")

few = pd.read_csv(data.data_dir() / "train.csv", usecols=["id", "Crop_Type", "Irrigation_Need"], nrows=5, index_col="id")
few

read 630,000 rows × 21 columns in 0.32 s

id

2.2 Writing CSV¶

A small summary is written out and read back, to show that the round trip keeps the data (and that index=False matters).

In [5]:
from pathlib import Path
summary = train.groupby("Crop_Type")[["Soil_Moisture", "Temperature_C", "Rainfall_mm"]].mean().round(2)
out = Path("crop_summary.csv")
summary.to_csv(out)
back = pd.read_csv(out, index_col="Crop_Type")
print(out.read_text()[:200])
print("identical after the round trip:", back.equals(summary))
out.unlink()

Crop_Type,Soil_Moisture,Temperature_C,Rainfall_mm

Maize,37.17,27.02,1465.16
Potato,37.08,27.11,1458.01

Inspection already shows the two facts that shape everything later: there are no missing values, and the classes are imbalanced (High is only 3.3%).

4. Selecting and filtering data¶

4.1 loc vs iloc¶

loc selects by label (index values and column names); iloc selects by position. With the default RangeIndex they look the same, until the index changes.

In [10]:
print(train.loc[0:2, ["Crop_Type", "Soil_Moisture"]])      # labels 0, 1 AND 2 (inclusive)
print(train.iloc[0:2, [11, 3]])                          # positions 0 and 1 (end excluded)

by_id = train.set_index("id").sort_values("Soil_Moisture")
print("\nafter sorting, loc and iloc pick different rows:")
print(by_id.loc[[0]][["Soil_Moisture"]])
print(by_id.iloc[[0]][["Soil_Moisture"]])

4.2 Filtering (boolean indexing)¶

In [11]:
dry_hot = train[(train["Soil_Moisture"] < 20) & (train["Temperature_C"] > 35)]
print(f"{len(dry_hot):,} dry and hot fields")
print(dry_hot["Irrigation_Need"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))

print("\nrice or sugarcane in the flowering stage:")
q = train[train["Crop_Type"].isin(["Rice", "Sugarcane"]) & (train["Crop_Growth_Stage"] == "Flowering")]
print(q["Irrigation_Need"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))

print("\nthe same with query():", len(train.query("Soil_Moisture < 20 and Temperature_C > 35")))

Filtering alone finds a strong rule: among dry, hot fields, High is many times more common than its 3.3% overall share.

Group-by is the other everyday tool:

In [12]:
(train.groupby(["Crop_Growth_Stage", "Mulching_Used"])["Irrigation_Need"]
      .value_counts(normalize=True).unstack().round(3))

5. Data visualisation with Matplotlib¶

5.1 Line plot¶

The share of High fields as soil moisture goes up, computed in moisture bins.

In [13]:
train["moisture_bin"] = pd.cut(train["Soil_Moisture"], bins=np.arange(0, 70, 2.5))
share = train.groupby("moisture_bin", observed=True)["Irrigation_Need"].value_counts(normalize=True).unstack()
mid = [b.mid for b in share.index]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls in data.CLASSES:
    ax.plot(mid, share[cls], marker="o", ms=4, label=cls, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS[cls])
ax.set(xlabel="soil moisture (%)", ylabel="share of fields", title="Irrigation need by soil moisture")
ax.legend(title="need")
plotting.save("g02-line")
plt.show()

5.2 Bar plot¶

In [14]:
counts = train.groupby("Crop_Type")["Irrigation_Need"].value_counts().unstack()[data.CLASSES]
ax = counts.plot.bar(stacked=True, color=COLORS, rot=0)
ax.set(ylabel="fields", title="Fields per crop, by irrigation need")
plotting.save("g02-bar")
plt.show()

5.3 Histogram¶

In [15]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls in data.CLASSES:
    ax.hist(train.loc[train["Irrigation_Need"] == cls, "Temperature_C"], bins=40, alpha=0.6,
            density=True, label=cls, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS[cls])
ax.set(xlabel="temperature (°C)", ylabel="density", title="Temperature distribution per class")
ax.legend()
plotting.save("g02-hist")
plt.show()

5.4 Scatter plot¶

In [16]:
s = data.sample(6000, seed=2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls in data.CLASSES:
    part = s[s["Irrigation_Need"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(part["Soil_Moisture"], part["Temperature_C"], s=8, alpha=0.5, label=cls, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS[cls])
ax.set(xlabel="soil moisture (%)", ylabel="temperature (°C)", title="High need sits in the dry, hot corner")
ax.legend(markerscale=3)
plotting.save("g02-scatter")
plt.show()

5.5 Pie chart¶

Pie charts are only good for a few parts of one whole, which is exactly the class balance:

In [17]:
vc = train["Irrigation_Need"].value_counts()[data.CLASSES]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4.5))
ax.pie(vc, labels=vc.index, colors=COLORS, autopct="%1.1f%%", startangle=90, wedgeprops={"edgecolor": "white"})
ax.set_title("Class balance")
plotting.save("g02-pie")
plt.show()

6. Customising plots¶

Titles, labels, limits, ticks, annotations, reference lines, styles and colours. The same scatter, made to make one point:

In [18]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.8))
high = s[s["Irrigation_Need"] == "High"]
rest = s[s["Irrigation_Need"] != "High"]
ax.scatter(rest["Soil_Moisture"], rest["Temperature_C"], s=6, color="#cbd5e1", label="Low or Medium")
ax.scatter(high["Soil_Moisture"], high["Temperature_C"], s=14, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS["High"], edgecolor="white", lw=0.4, label="High")
ax.axvline(25, ls="--", color=plotting.ACCENT, lw=1)
ax.axhline(30, ls="--", color=plotting.ACCENT, lw=1)
ax.fill_betweenx([30, 45], 0, 25, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS["High"], alpha=0.07)
ax.annotate(f"{len(high[(high.Soil_Moisture < 25) & (high.Temperature_C > 30)]) / len(high):.0%} of High fields\nare in this box",
            xy=(12, 38), xytext=(38, 41), fontsize=10, arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "color": plotting.ACCENT})
ax.set(xlim=(0, 65), ylim=(10, 45), xlabel="soil moisture (%)", ylabel="temperature (°C)")
ax.set_title("Dry and hot fields need the most water", loc="left")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=True)
plotting.save("g02-custom")
plt.show()

7. Subplots¶

A grid of small plots that share axes is the fastest way to compare many features:

In [19]:
features = ["Soil_Moisture", "Temperature_C", "Rainfall_mm", "Wind_Speed_kmh", "Humidity", "Soil_pH"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=False)
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, features):
    for cls in data.CLASSES:
        ax.hist(train.loc[train["Irrigation_Need"] == cls, col], bins=30, histtype="step", lw=1.6,
                density=True, color=plotting.CLASS_COLORS[cls], label=cls)
    ax.set_title(col.replace("_", " "), fontsize=10)
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("Which features separate the classes?", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g02-subplots")
plt.show()

Soil moisture, temperature, rainfall and wind speed shift clearly between classes; humidity and pH barely move. That's a hypothesis for the next notebook to test properly.
